title: Short-Term Urban Traffic Volume Forecasting Using XGBoost: A Metropolitan Freeway Case Study

abstract.Purpose: This study evaluates how accurately XGBoost forecasts short-term hourly traffic volume on a metropolitan freeway and considers how such forecasts could inform data-driven traffic management. Optimisation is not tested.
abstract.Design/methodology/approach: Hourly volume and weather records for Interstate 94 in Minnesota (2012–2018) were converted into lag, rolling, calendar and weather features. XGBoost was compared with random forest, ridge regression and seasonal baselines at 1-, 3-, 6- and 24-hour horizons, using a chronological split (test period October 2017–September 2018), time-series cross-validation and block-bootstrap intervals.
abstract.Findings: One hour ahead, XGBoost reached an RMSE of 222 vehicles/h (R² 0.987), against 494 for the best seasonal baseline; error rose to 384 at 24 hours. Random forest performed equivalently and was slightly better at 3 and 6 hours, so an XGBoost advantage was not established. Recent observations drove short-horizon accuracy; weather added no measurable gain.
abstract.Research limitations/implications: Evidence comes from one detector on one freeway, with extended data gaps. Results may not transfer to urban street networks. Volume forecasting is not congestion or accident-risk prediction.
abstract.Practical implications: Short-horizon forecasts could support monitoring dashboards and incident-response planning on comparable corridors, subject to validation on live data.
abstract.Social implications: Aggregated counts raise few privacy concerns, but forecast errors could mislead decisions, so benefits should be assessed across all road users.
abstract.Originality/value: A transparent, leakage-controlled open-data benchmark of XGBoost against tuned random forest and seasonal baselines, with uncertainty intervals, reporting where XGBoost does not outperform simpler alternatives.

locator: This paper examines short-term forecasting of hourly traffic volume on a metropolitan freeway using XGBoost, a gradient-boosted decision-tree method, and compares it with random forest, ridge regression and seasonal baseline forecasts. Using an open dataset of hourly Interstate 94 traffic volume and weather observations, it builds lag, rolling-window, calendar and weather features, tunes models with time-series cross-validation, and evaluates them on a held-out final year at horizons of 1, 3, 6 and 24 hours. It reports accuracy, uncertainty intervals, feature ablations and SHAP-based interpretation, and discusses how such forecasts could support data-driven traffic management. The work is relevant to researchers in machine learning for transportation, intelligent transportation systems, traffic forecasting and explainable machine learning, and to practitioners in traffic operations and urban mobility analytics.
